nodes.title: The Call of Lady Wisdom

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 1:7 makes the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge. Within chapters 1-9, what is that fear?
options: A dread of punishment that keeps young people in line
A reverent trust that bends the whole life toward God
A polite respect paid before getting on to practical skill
A beginner's stage that real wisdom eventually outgrows
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 3:5-7 unfolds the fear as wholehearted trust in the LORD joined to turning from evil.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 3:5-8 again. Notice what the fear of the LORD is paired with and what it produces.

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 9 closes the section with Wisdom and Folly each hosting a feast and calling to the simple. What does the parallel staging teach?
options: The simple may safely sample both tables before they choose
Wisdom's feast is reserved for the already learned few
The choice between the two can wait until later in life
Folly borrows wisdom's own voice, so the difference shows in destinations
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 9:4 and 9:16 give both hostesses the same call, and Proverbs 9:18 shows where one banquet ends.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 9:4-6 and 9:16-18 again. Notice what the two invitations share, and where they part.

nodes.summary: A father's extended appeal to his son — and Wisdom personified as a woman calling in the streets, present with God at creation itself, while Folly seduces from the other doorway. 'The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom' is the book's thesis and the whole genre's foundation.

connections.reason: Wisdom beside God at creation (Prov 8) is key background to John's Word who was with God in the beginning.
Paul's 'Christ the wisdom of God' takes up this book's central figure.

nodes.discussion_prompt: In these chapters wisdom is a woman shouting in the streets, pleading with everyone who passes to stop and listen. Why does the book picture wisdom calling out in public rather than waiting to be found, and what in your daily life tends to drown her voice out?
assessment_questions: According to Proverbs 1:7 and 9:10, what is the beginning of wisdom, and who is pictured calling out in the streets in these chapters?
The father keeps setting two paths before his son, one leading to life and one to ruin. Why does Proverbs treat everyday choices about friends, money, and desire as a choice between those two paths?
Proverbs 4:23 says to guard your heart above all else, because everything you do flows from it. What is shaping your heart right now, and what would guarding it actually require this week?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Reverent awe and trust toward God is the starting point of all wisdom, and it produces humility and obedience rather than terror.

Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling in the streets and singing that she was there before creation began; the poetry has been read in several ways across history, and its invitation is the point: whoever finds wisdom finds life.
The father's repeated appeals show that heeding trustworthy counsel and accepting loving discipline guards a young life.
Folly leads to ruin and obedience leads to life, so the choices made in youth shape the whole course of a life.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain in your own words what the fear of the LORD means and why Proverbs calls it the beginning of wisdom.

nodes.title: The Proverbs of Solomon
nodes.summary: The collection announced at Proverbs 10:1: hundreds of self-contained two-line sayings, most setting the righteous and the wicked, the wise and the fool, side by side. The subjects are unglamorous and universal, money, speech, work, anger, honesty, friendship, and the sayings describe how life ordinarily runs under God's order rather than issuing guarantees. Read slowly, a few at a time, they train judgment; read as promises, they break.

prerequisites.reason: The prologue supplies the interpretive key — fear of the LORD — without which the sayings flatten into fortune-cookie advice.

connections.reason: James is the New Testament's proverbs collection; its teaching on the tongue distills these chapters.

nodes.discussion_prompt: These chapters keep returning to the tongue: gentle answers, rash words, gossip, the timely word. Think back over your last week of talking and typing. Which saying about speech names something you actually watched happen, and what would taking it seriously cost you?
assessment_questions: What does Proverbs 15:1 say a gentle answer does, and what does a harsh word stir up?

Proverbs keeps linking diligence, honesty, and patience to blessing, yet everyone knows honest people who suffer. What kind of truth are these sayings claiming to be, and how should that shape the way we use them?
Proverbs 13:20 says whoever walks with the wise becomes wise. Who are the people you spend the most time with, and what are they making you?

teaching_concepts.concept: Proverbs describe how life usually works
teaching_concepts.explanation: These sayings state reliable patterns of God's moral order rather than guarantees, so wise readers hold them with humility when life brings exceptions.
Speech can build up life or tear down people and reputations, so guarding the tongue is one of the most practical forms of wisdom.
Small daily habits of honest work, patience, and self-control shape a future far more than sudden dramatic changes.
Sayings like Proverbs 16:9 set human planning under the LORD's direction, holding responsibility and God's governance together in a single couplet without strain.

nodes.completion_criteria: Explain the difference between reading a proverb as a guarantee and reading it as a pattern, using one saying about speech or money as your example.

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 10:4 links diligent hands to wealth. How does this collection mean sayings like that to be read?
options: As covenant promises God is bound to keep for the faithful
As folk observations the rest of Scripture later corrects
As rewards reserved for the righteous in the life to come
As patterns of how life usually works under God's order
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 16:9 holds the collection's balance: humans plan, the LORD directs the steps, so the sayings describe patterns under providence.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 10:4 beside 15:16 and 16:8. Notice what the same collection says is better than great wealth.

comprehension_check.question: Why does this collection return so often to the power of the tongue?
options: Because eloquent speech is the surest path to advancement
Because words carry real power to build or destroy lives
Because silence is presented as safer than any speech at all
Because the fool's speech is what exposes him to punishment
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 18:21 grounds the collection's speech-ethic: the tongue holds death and life, which is why so many sayings weigh words.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 12:18 and 18:21 again. Notice what the tongue is compared to and what it is said to hold.

nodes.title: The Sayings of the Wise
nodes.summary: At Proverbs 22:17 the book announces a new collection, thirty sayings shaped as a teacher's counsel and aimed, it says, at settling the reader's trust in the LORD. The form changes with the source: instead of stand-alone couplets, these are multi-verse admonitions with reasons attached, do not exploit the poor, do not wear yourself out for wealth, do not envy sinners, rescue those being led toward death, capped by two vivid cautionary scenes, the drunkard and the sluggard's ruined field. A short appendix of further sayings of the wise closes the collection.

prerequisites.reason: The Sayings of the Wise follow the Solomonic collection as the book's next collection.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Three times these sayings tell the reader not to envy sinners or the wicked. Why does envy of people who seem to be winning get treated as such a spiritual emergency, and where does that envy get traction in you?
assessment_questions: Where does this collection announce itself, and what does the teacher say in Proverbs 22:19-21 that he wants the sayings to produce in the reader?
The sluggard's field in Proverbs 24:30-34 is a scene, not a command: the writer looks, considers, and receives instruction. What does that way of teaching assume about how wisdom is learned?

Proverbs 23:4-5 pictures wealth flying off like an eagle, yet tells you to restrain yourself, not to stop working. What would restraint without laziness look like in your work and spending this month?

teaching_concepts.explanation: The collection states its goal up front: not information but a reader whose confidence rests in the LORD, since skill in living flows from that anchor.
Unlike bare couplets, these sayings argue their case, warning against exploiting the poor because the LORD himself takes up their cause, so wisdom can give an account of itself.
Riches are pictured taking flight like an eagle, so exhausting yourself to catch them is folly, and contentment becomes realism rather than resignation.
The drunkard and the sluggard's overgrown field teach by portrait rather than command, training the reader to watch a life and draw the lesson.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe how the Sayings of the Wise differ in form from the couplets of chapters 10-22, and explain the purpose the collection announces for itself in Proverbs 22:17-21.

comprehension_check.question: The Sayings of the Wise open with a purpose statement. What do they aim to produce?
options: A reader whose trust is settled on the LORD
A son able to succeed in the royal court
A scribe trained to answer with polished words
A household kept safe from poverty and disgrace
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 22:19 states the collection's own purpose: these sayings exist so that your trust may be in the LORD.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 22:17-19 again. Notice the reason the teacher gives for passing these sayings on today.

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 24:16 says the righteous man falls seven times. What distinguishes him from the wicked here?
options: He falls fewer times than the wicked man does
He gets up again, while calamity fells the wicked
He is spared the schemes the wicked lay for him
His falls are lighter because the LORD cushions them
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 24:16 marks the righteous by resilience, rising after every fall, rather than by never falling.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 24:15-16 again. Notice what the righteous man does after each fall, and what happens to the wicked in trouble.

nodes.title: Hezekiah's Collection

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 26:4 and 26:5 give opposite instructions back to back about answering a fool. What does the pairing teach about proverbs?
options: One saying corrects the other and quietly replaces it
The collectors failed to notice an obvious contradiction
A proverb is a tool fitted to its moment by judgment
The safest reading is to never engage a fool at all
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 26:4-5 keeps both sayings because each guards against a different harm, and wisdom reads the moment.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 26:4-5 again. Notice the different danger each verse names in its second half.

comprehension_check.question: Proverbs 25:1 notes that Hezekiah's men copied out more of Solomon's proverbs centuries later. What does that header reveal?
options: Wisdom was deliberately curated and handed down the generations
The collection had been lost until Hezekiah's reign recovered it
Wisdom writing in Israel ended when Solomon's era passed
A king's approval is what makes a proverb count as true
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 25:1 shows a later generation at work preserving earlier wisdom so it could keep on teaching.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 25:1 again. Notice who is handling the sayings and how much time separates them from Solomon.

nodes.summary: More Solomonic sayings, copied out centuries later by 'the men of Hezekiah' — sharper and more political: fools and their folly, sluggards on their hinges, kings and courts, 'as iron sharpens iron.' Evidence inside the Bible of how wisdom was curated and transmitted.

prerequisites.reason: Same genre and voice; the earlier collections establish the form these extend.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Proverbs 27:17 says iron sharpens iron, and one person sharpens another. Sharpening involves friction. Who in your life is close enough and honest enough to sharpen you, and what makes that kind of friendship so rare?
assessment_questions: Who copied out this collection of Solomon's proverbs according to Proverbs 25:1, and what kinds of people do these chapters keep returning to?

Proverbs 26:4 says do not answer a fool according to his folly, and the very next verse says answer a fool according to his folly. Why would the collectors place those sayings side by side, and what does the pairing teach about how proverbs work?

Proverbs 28:13 says whoever conceals his sins will not prosper, while the one who confesses and forsakes them finds mercy. What would it look like this week to stop concealing a failure, and who would you confess it to?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Hezekiah's scribes copied these sayings centuries after Solomon, showing that God's people worked to curate wisdom and hand it on.
The back-to-back sayings about answering a fool show that applying a proverb well means reading the situation, since wisdom fits words to moments.
These chapters tie the justice and restraint of rulers to the wellbeing of everyone under them, so character in leadership is a public matter.
Honest friends, welcomed rebuke, and confessed failure are the rough surfaces God uses to sharpen a person.

nodes.completion_criteria: Retell what Proverbs 26:4-5 does with the fool, and explain why applying a proverb well takes discernment about the situation.

nodes.title: Agur, Lemuel, and the Woman of Valor

comprehension_check.question: Agur opens Proverbs 30 confessing how little he knows, then asks for neither poverty nor riches. What links the confession and the prayer?
options: Both treat learning and wealth as corrupting in themselves
Both perform a modesty designed to be admired by others
Both give up on wisdom ever being found by anyone
Both practice dependence that never outgrows its need of God
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 30:8-9 gives the prayer's logic, fearing both the fullness that forgets God and the poverty that dishonors him.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 30:7-9 again. Notice the reason Agur attaches to each half of his request.

comprehension_check.question: The book ends with an alphabet poem about a capable woman running a household (Proverbs 31:10-31). Why close a wisdom book there?
options: It narrows wisdom's true arena down to marriage and home
It shows the book's wisdom embodied in ordinary daily work
It rewards the patient reader with a portrait of ideal beauty
It hands wives a checklist their households must fully satisfy
comprehension_check.why: Proverbs 31:30 lands the poem on the book's thesis, praise for the woman who fears the LORD.
comprehension_check.hint: Read Proverbs 31:30 again. Notice which trait the poem singles out for praise and which ones it sets aside.

nodes.summary: Two outsider voices close the book: Agur's humble numerical riddles ('three things are too wonderful for me'), King Lemuel's mother on power and its temptations, and the alphabet-poem portrait of the woman of valor — wisdom from chapters 1-9 no longer personified but embodied in an actual household.

prerequisites.reason: The valiant woman of 31 deliberately mirrors Lady Wisdom of 1-9 — the book's frame closes.

connections.reason: Boaz calls Ruth a 'woman of valor' — the only narrative character given Proverbs 31's exact title; in the Hebrew ordering Ruth follows Proverbs directly.

nodes.discussion_prompt: Agur asks God for neither poverty nor riches, just his daily portion, because either extreme could pull his heart away from God. What would it mean for you to pray that prayer honestly, and which half of it would be harder to mean?
assessment_questions: What two things does Agur ask God for in Proverbs 30:7-9, and what does Lemuel's mother tell the king to do for those who cannot speak for themselves?

The woman of valor works, trades, plants, gives to the poor, and laughs at the days to come, and the poem ends by praising the woman who fears the LORD. How does this closing portrait show what the wisdom of chapters 1 to 9 looks like when someone actually lives it?
Proverbs 31:8-9 commands speaking up for the voiceless and defending the poor. Who has no voice in the rooms you are in, and what would opening your mouth for them cost you?

teaching_concepts.explanation: Agur confesses how little he knows and asks only for daily bread, modeling a wisdom that begins with admitting limits.
Agur warns against adding to God's words, because every word of God proves true and shields those who take refuge in him.
Lemuel's mother teaches that a ruler's strength is for defending the poor and the voiceless rather than for indulging himself.
The woman of valor shows the book's wisdom lived out in an ordinary household through work, generosity, and the fear of the LORD.

nodes.completion_criteria: Describe the woman of valor of Proverbs 31 and explain how she embodies the fear of the LORD taught at the start of the book.
